episode_thesis: Carver argues that systematic means literally following the system: overriding signals makes a strategy untestable, so discretion should be confined to what and when to buy while speed, exits and position size stay rule-based, and parameter fitting should default to none (or the average of individual, asset-class and global fits) to avoid overfitting. He and Kaastrup-Larsen add that the Simplify CTA ETF's switch to an energy-only book betrays what investors bought, that AI in quant research chiefly adds overfitting and code-oversight risk, that trend speed should not be changed with the VIX because high volatility comes in V-shaped, secular and rapid-V forms with different optimal speeds, and that bond-market stress could revive bond trends.

speakers.name: Rob Carver
speakers.role: Independent systematic futures trader, author of books on systematic trading and co-host of the Systematic Investor series; formerly at AHL
speakers.speaker_note: Caption spells the host 'Neils Castro Razen'. Tuesday-to-Thursday timing: data quoted by the host are as of Tuesday of the recording week (mid-September 2026). worldview_premises.premise: Systematic trading means mechanically following the system; overriding signals when inconvenient makes the system impossible to test and is the worst way to mix discretion and systematics.
worldview_premises.support: Definition of the word and the testability argument; he reacted to an X post saying systematic does not mean blindly taking every setup.

worldview_premises.premise: Retail traders lose mainly through position, cost and risk-management errors, not entries alone: about 95% lose money rather than the roughly half that coin-flip entries would give.
worldview_premises.support: Stated statistic (95% of retail traders, worse for day traders).

worldview_premises.premise: Skill in entries and skill in exits are separate; mutual fund managers pick stocks well but exit poorly.
worldview_premises.support: Academic research he cannot name; study of retail and institutional long-only managers.

worldview_premises.premise: Fitting rule weights per instrument is overfitting (noise, little signal), while fitting by asset class or pooled across all instruments does about as well; with few instruments (for example 2 bonds, 3 equities, 1 FX) one should not fit by asset class.
worldview_premises.support: His blog-post series on pooling and optimization, tested on his many-instrument data set.

worldview_premises.premise: The most robust approach is to average the individual, asset-class and global fits (equivalent to putting a third of risk in each), since one cannot know which explanation is right; it has about 0.98-0.99 correlation with global-only fitting.
worldview_premises.support: Meta-fitting argument and his own comparison.

worldview_premises.premise: Whether to use different rule weights by asset class was partly an organisational-politics question (asset-class research teams protective of their P&L) and should instead be an empirical question tested on data.
worldview_premises.support: His AHL experience managing the fixed-income team.

worldview_premises.premise: Complex matrix fits (for example allocating to fast trend in cheap, diversifying markets even if it does not make money there) add complexity with little value.
AI in quant research mainly risks overfitting, and AI-written code needs guard rails and human oversight; governance applies to AI-assisted systems as it does to others.
worldview_premises.support: An AI code review of his research code found a serious bug but introduced a worse one that would have deleted all short positions.

worldview_premises.premise: Consumer-grade AI trading may raise turnover, risk and volatility, but evidence is too early; uninformed AI-driven retail herds create opportunities to trade the other side.
worldview_premises.support: Speculation drawn from the social-media environment and meme-stock analogies.

worldview_premises.premise: LLMs recommend large trend-following allocations because their training text, including this podcast, advocates it, so their advice is circular.
Published research should be revisited after about 10 years for out-of-sample evidence.
worldview_premises.support: Alpha Architect VIX and trend update; Lasse Pedersen's 100-year trend paper.

worldview_premises.premise: High volatility is not one thing: it may be 2008 (a secular turn), COVID 2020 (a wider V) or the 2025 tariff tantrum (a very quick V), each with a different optimal trend speed, and one cannot know ahead which.
worldview_premises.support: Reading of the three episodes; he notes figures from the tariff tantrum and COVID.

worldview_premises.premise: High volatility does not simply help trend following as the straddle intuition suggests; results depend on trend speed, reaction speed and trading speed.
worldview_premises.support: His own parallel finding that trend does less well when volatility is high.

worldview_premises.premise: Classic quant factors (value, momentum) did badly in the 2018-2020 quant winter, factor R-squared in manager returns varies over 25 years, and quant equity managers differ rather than simply holding basic factors, so diversification across managers works except in crowded events.
worldview_premises.support: Man Group Insights note read that morning.

decision_process.practice: Default to no fitting; fit only with strong, robust, out-of-sample evidence; avoid per-instrument fits; prefer the average of individual, asset-class and global fits, planning to move his own approach from global-only toward it.
decision_process.why: Building something to last in an unknown future from historical data invites overfitting.

decision_process.practice: Follow the system's signals; where discretion is retained, limit it to what to buy and when.
Make trading speed, exits and position size rule-based; if exits stay discretionary, use a simple stop-loss and allow discretionary exits only with a significant skill track record.
decision_process.why: Cost and risk management are science, not art.

decision_process.practice: Non-leveraged traders must rank positions and follow path-dependent swap rules; the biggest debate is whether to resize positions for volatility after entry or let them ride.
decision_process.why: Without leverage not all signals can be taken.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Carver's account of the Simplify ETF is based only on a Seeking Alpha article, which he says he assumes is correct.
Carver attributes the study that fund managers exit poorly to unnamed academics.
Carver says he sees no evidence on the market impact of consumer-grade AI trading, yet speculates opportunities to trade against herds; no capture method is given.
Carver's view that the market is poised for a shock is explicitly qualitative, with no statistics.
Carver plans to add instrument and asset-class information to his global-only fit but says the change would be minor (0.98-0.99 correlation), which weakens the case for urgency.
Carver's own risk is a third of average and flat YTD after strong early weeks, while indices are up 12%, so his results are not representative.
Carver reports the Alpha Architect update says VIX-dependent speed still works, but also that he trades less momentum in high volatility, the opposite direction to the article's speed-up.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observables named: Treasury and Norwegian fund bond actions and yields (bond trend), the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve reaching its limit, US midterms and the new Fed chair's policy, momentum in equities, and manager-level style stability. Carver sees no forecast, only a sense of poise before a shock; horizon is weeks to the year-end.
reader_inferences: (reader) Carver's rules reduce degrees of freedom: no per-instrument fitting, no discretionary exits, no VIX-based speed, which are all ways of keeping out-of-sample performance close to backtest.
(reader) His speed-versus-V-shape argument is that medium speed is the worst exposure in a V because it neither avoids nor rides it.
(reader) The ETF episode is read by both speakers as a governance and expectations problem rather than a performance problem.
